comments.author: mitchellh

These are Ghostty GUI release notes, but I want to take a moment to highlight the libghostty progress we've made since Ghostty 1.3.
As a reminder, libghostty is the highly portable, embeddable library that provides core terminal emulation, render state, and more. I always felt that a free, high qualty, lightweight, reusable terminal emulation core would benefit the developer world more than any single GUI application. And that is playing out!
It is and always was my true purpose with the Ghostty project (I said this in my first ever talk about Ghostty!). I've jokingly said many times that Ghostty GUI is just a glorified tech demo for libghostty. That's not fair though, because GUI is great and there are really talented people working on it.
Since I started the project, Ghostty has always gotten people saying "I don't understand why you'd start a terminal emulator today." Well, the answer is libghostty. It's truly unique and its enabling something special (imo!).
Highlights of libghostty since 6 months ago (none of the below was true 6 months ago):
- Libghostty has nearly 100% coverage of all of Ghostty's core (and you can compile with flags to remove any of these features for size/

stories.title_en: Python's experimental JIT to be removed

comments.author: adrian17
comments.text:
Unfortunate. I've been following the work on it occasionally.
On one hand, it seemed like JIT work was really progressing in high gear until SC requested a new PEP. Also unfortunate, as it seemed like part of the hope for the JIT was that it'd counter the performance penalty from free threading.
On the other, it did feel (to me) like with all the fancy (and definitely cool) optimizations it got (automatic refcount operation removal, new type-based specializations, inplace math operations), the macrobenchmark benefits weren't _that_ exciting for a JIT. It definitely has potential for more, maybe with even fancier optimizations like unboxing ints, but the complexity just keeps going up.
> It said that the PEP was "overly optimistic" about user-visible differences with the JIT enabled.
The JIT is technically generated from the same source as the interpreter loop itself, so originally the differences were extremely unlikely, but I imagine the risk just kept going up as new JIT-only paths and optimizations were introduced.
And politically, I feel like SC’s reasoning was just “this side project has landed in main branch almost by accident and has been stewing without oversight ever since

comments.author: rich_sasha
comments.text:
Here’s an idea instead (maybe it already exists). Allow a decorator for writing inline Cython. It solves, I think, 90% of the problem. On first run, or eagerly, compile the decorated functions. Basically, Cython is the JIT, and user enables it explicitly.
This way I can easily write inlined functions with proper C speed, in a Python esque language.
Reasons why I rarely use Cython without this:
- unmodified Python code running in Cython is often faster, but not that much. 50% or so is my rule of thumb.
- but the development style is very different for Cython and Python, adding a lot of impedance. Eg reloading doesn’t quite work, profiling is different, you need a build directory and a build step at deployment etc.
- Cython proper is different enough and I’d argue unintuitive enough that if I have to have all these things in place, I might as well wrap my function in Rust.
Such a decorator would give you a low friction way to make things faster when you need it, with scope for making it much faster via all the funny Cython, while keeping Python-esque semantics, in particular "development semantics".
I think it would require some language modification since Cython was definitely a sup

A sad day for CPython but it doesn't have to be a sad day for Python. There is a fully maintained implementation of Python 3.13 that has an advanced JIT compiler. https://graalpy.org/
A bit like Chrome there's a fully open source version and a proprietary version with a few extra bells and whistles, but the latter is entirely free for both open and commercial usage (you can't redistribute it for a fee). So you may as well use it.
It has other interesting features
• Scalable pauseless GC
• Single binary distribution of Python programs (like Go)
• Fancy and optimized interop with other languages including Java, JavaScript, Kotlin, Ruby and any other Truffle language.
• Supports native extensions. Tested and works with common libs like SciPy, NumPy, PyTorch, Pandas etc:
https://graalpy.org/python-developers/compatibility/
• They're working on a GIL-free mode
In recent weeks there has been a release of a new web framework for Python that only runs on GraalPy, called Pyronaut (
https://pyronaut.io/

comments.author: mrothroc

This matches my own experience, pre-AI. As I've moved from IC to having a team over the years, more code was being written than I could possibly understand at the depth I would have if I'd written it myself.
The skill I learned is exactly as you describe: understand the system. For me, this means "boxes and lines", the components and how they interact. I've encouraged developers on my team to make sequence diagrams part of their deliverable, because it helps both of us put the code in the context of the system.
The boxes can be opaque because I know the boundaries and expected inputs and outputs. This tells me when I need to go in a box: is it sending a malformed message? I can trace that back into the code.
I think that's the skill we have to cultivate now that coding agents produce far more than we can review line-by-line. The system view is the map, and the boundaries tell us where to go hunting inside the box.

Stressed and uncomfortable developers have, historically, been a leading indicator of product failure. Software is complex and when devs can't handle the breadth of ownership + the depth of expertise at the same time, it means bad work that leads to product failure. It's not clear that agents fail in the same way, or that our collective intuition about how and when to trust agents is sufficiently developed to predict product failure in the same way.
As anecdata: I know a bunch of growth-SaaS/last-batch-of-IPO companies where the devs are all stressed, the feature ship rate is up, and incidents are down. All at the same time.
So yes, quick learners and just-in-time depth is important, but so is intuition about where discomfort is going to produce true failure. comments.author: theptip
comments.text:
> Throw nine autonomous agents at a single codebase without crystal-clear orchestration, and they will happily rewrite each other's work in a high-speed loop.
Mm, I think this is quite overstated in the era of Opus 5 / Sol.
What we actually see is that agents are much better at coordinating than humans. Numbers from OpenAI show 4x the agents gives 2x the speed.
Of course, for truly single-threaded tasks you can’t gain much by parallelizing, but ask Fable/Astra to chop a big task into small pieces, write the APIs first, then sub-agents take what’s behind the API, and you’ll usually get a much better speedup than if you asked humans to work this way.
In practice most big projects have crux choke points and then fanout migration/buildout phases.
Even on the cruxes, where you need a single decision, agents don’t have ego and so you can get speedups by eg. asking for 10 clean room implementations of the same problem, and have a judge model pick the best; this can let you go much faster, and no human team would put up with that collaboration model.
